title: How to Measure the ROI of Your Identity Verification and Fraud Prevention Stack
summary: Learn how to calculate identity verification and fraud prevention ROI, measure avoided fraud losses, track onboarding costs and build a business case.
body_markdown:
Your business spends millions on identity verification, fraud detection, and manual reviews every year. Fraud losses may be falling, and onboarding may be getting faster, but when finance asks what that investment has actually returned, the numbers are not always easy to produce.


The challenge is that fraud prevention creates value in different ways. Some benefits are visible, such as fewer manual reviews or higher onboarding completion rates. Others, like fraud losses that never occurred, are harder to measure. A credible ROI calculation needs to account for both without overstating the savings.


Here's how to calculate the cost of your identity verification and fraud prevention stack, measure its financial returns and identify the metrics that matter to your finance team.


### 1. Calculate the Full Cost of Your Verification and Fraud Prevention Stack


Start with everything your business spends to operate its identity verification and fraud prevention systems.


The subscription fee or cost per verification is only part of the investment.


Cost category What to include


API and platform fees Verification charges, fraud monitoring fees and subscriptions


Integration and maintenance Developer hours, implementation and ongoing technical support


Fraud operations Analyst salaries, manual reviews and investigations


Vendor management Compliance reviews, procurement, contracts and vendor support


False positives Additional review expenses and lost contribution margin from legitimate customers incorrectly rejected or discouraged from completing onboarding


Separate one-time implementation expenses from recurring operating costs. When calculating quarterly ROI, allocate implementation costs consistently across the period used for the analysis.


A business paying ₦3 million in verification fees might assume that's its fraud prevention budget. Add ₦2 million in analyst salaries, plus developer time and vendor management, and the actual cost is considerably higher.


Also, make sure the same financial impact is not counted twice. If you include additional customer contribution from improved onboarding as a benefit, do not count the recovery of that same contribution again as a reduction in false-positive costs.


A complete cost calculation gives finance a reliable starting point.


### 2. Identify the Four Sources of Financial Return


Identity verification and fraud prevention create value in different parts of the business.


Some returns come from preventing losses. Others come from reducing manual work or helping more customers complete onboarding.


#### **A. Fraud losses avoided**


Fraud prevention reduces the cost of fraudulent onboarding, account takeovers, unauthorised transactions and other financial abuse.


To estimate avoided fraud losses, compare your fraud loss rate against a credible baseline using a consistent measure of transaction value or customer activity.


For example, suppose a fintech processes ₦2 billion in transaction value during a quarter.


Its historical fraud loss rate is 0.8%, while its current loss rate is 0.3%.


At the historical rate, expected fraud losses would be ₦16 million. At the current rate, losses would be ₦6 million.


That gives an estimated **₦10 million reduction in quarterly fraud losses** .


However, a lower fraud loss rate does not automatically mean the verification or fraud prevention stack caused the entire reduction. Changes in transaction mix, customer behaviour, seasonal activity and broader fraud trends can also influence the results.


For a more reliable comparison, use consistent reporting periods and account for significant changes in transaction activity. Where possible, compare similar customer groups or transaction segments. Allow time for delayed fraud reports and chargebacks before finalising the figures.


Fraud also creates costs beyond the amount stolen.


The[LexisNexis Risk Solutions True Cost of Fraud Study](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/global/en/about-us/press-room/press-release/20240417-true-cost-of-fraud-south-africa) found that every rand lost to fraud cost South African financial institutions R4.52 when associated expenses were included.


Those expenses can include investigation costs, administration, external fees and recovery efforts.


The South African study illustrates the wider cost of fraud, but businesses should calculate their own costs rather than applying its multiplier directly.


#### **B. Manual review costs saved**


Manual identity checks and fraud investigations consume staff time. Automation reduces the effort spent on routine checks and gives analysts more capacity to investigate complex cases.


Calculate the value of time saved using:


**Hours saved × Cost per staff hour = Value of staff capacity recovered**


Suppose a fraud operations team previously spent 600 hours reviewing routine verification cases every month.


After improving its verification workflow, that falls to 350 hours.


The team saves 250 hours monthly. At an average staff cost of ₦4,000 per hour, that represents ₦1 million in monthly staff capacity, or **₦3 million per quarter** .


There is an important distinction here.


If the business reduces overtime, outsourced review expenses or other actual expenditure, the reduction counts as a direct cost saving.


If employees use the recovered hours for other investigations, the value is a productivity benefit rather than a cash saving.


Both matter, but finance should see them separately.


#### **C. Additional customers successfully onboarded**


Fraud prevention should stop suspicious activity without unnecessarily blocking legitimate customers.


A verification process that is slow, complicated or prone to incorrect rejections can reduce onboarding completion. Improving the process helps more customers finish verification and begin using the product.


Measure how many customers successfully complete onboarding before and after workflow improvements. Then calculate the financial contribution from the additional customers who become active.


For example, a fintech receives 10,000 onboarding applications per month.


Its completion rate improves from 70% to 78%.


That creates 800 additional completed onboardings.


If 60% become active customers, the business gains 480 additional active customers.


At an expected contribution margin of ₦5,000 per active customer over the measurement period, the estimated incremental contribution is:


**480 × ₦5,000 = ₦2.4 million per month**


Over a quarter, that amounts to **₦7.2 million in estimated additional contribution** , assuming the same monthly performance continues.


This calculation uses contribution margin rather than total revenue because serving additional customers also creates costs.


It also assumes the improved onboarding process is responsible for the additional completions. The business should confirm this through consistent tracking and, where possible, comparisons between similar customer groups.


#### **D. Compliance and investigation efficiency**


Identity verification and fraud monitoring also support compliance operations.


Well-organised verification records, transaction monitoring information and investigation histories reduce the manual effort required to prepare reports, respond to reviews and investigate suspicious activity.


Measure the hours spent on these activities before and after workflow improvements.


Suppose a compliance team previously spent 80 hours each month preparing reports and gathering verification records.


After improving the process, that falls to 30 hours.


The team recovers 50 hours monthly.


At ₦4,000 per hour:


**50 hours × ₦4,000 = ₦200,000 per month**


Over a quarter, that's **₦600,000 in recovered staff capacity** .


As with manual review savings, this represents a productivity benefit unless it results in an actual reduction in expenditure.


When calculating this benefit, exclude any hours already counted under manual review savings.


### 3. Calculate Your Fraud Prevention ROI


Once you know the full investment cost and the value of the benefits, the calculation is straightforward.


**ROI (%) = \[(Total benefits − Total investment cost) ÷ Total investment cost\] × 100**


Let's bring together the examples from the previous section for one illustrative quarter.


### Quarterly ROI calculation for a Nigerian fintech


Benefit Quarterly value Classification


Estimated fraud losses avoided ₦10,000,000 Estimated avoided loss


Manual review capacity recovered ₦3,000,000 Productivity benefit


Additional onboarding contribution ₦7,200,000 Estimated financial contribution


Compliance reporting capacity recovered ₦600,000 Productivity benefit


**Total estimated benefits** **₦20,800,000**


Total investment cost ₦8,000,000 Investment


**Net estimated benefit** **₦12,800,000**


Using the formula:


**ROI = \[(₦20,800,000 − ₦8,000,000) ÷ ₦8,000,000\] × 100**


**Illustrative blended ROI = 160%**


This means that for every ₦1 invested, the business generated an estimated ₦1.60 in net financial and productivity benefits.


These figures are illustrative, not actual Dojah customer results.


### Separate financial returns from productivity benefits


The 160% calculation combines estimated financial returns with the value of staff capacity recovered.


That distinction matters when presenting ROI to finance.


Of the ₦20.8 million in estimated benefits:


- **₦17.2 million** comes from estimated avoided fraud losses and additional customer contribution.
- **₦3.6 million** represents the value of recovered staff capacity from manual reviews and compliance reporting.


If the recovered staff time does not reduce actual expenditure, it should not be presented as a cash saving.


Excluding the ₦3.6 million productivity benefit gives an **indicative financial ROI of 115%** , assuming the estimated fraud-loss reduction and additional customer contribution are fully attributable to the investment.


Neither calculation automatically represents realised cash ROI. The final reported figure should reflect the benefits the business can substantiate and attribute to the investment.


Presenting these figures separately gives finance a clearer picture of both financial performance and operational improvements.


### 4. Track the Metrics That Explain Your ROI


The ROI percentage tells finance what the investment returned. Operational metrics explain where that return came from.


Track these metrics consistently:


Metric What it tells you


Fraud loss rate How much transaction value is lost to confirmed fraud


Fraud detection rate What proportion of confirmed fraudulent activity was detected


False positive rate How often legitimate activity is incorrectly flagged


Approval rate What proportion of verification or transaction requests is approved


Manual review rate What percentage of cases requires human intervention


Average verification time How quickly customers receive a verification decision


Onboarding completion rate How many applicants successfully finish verification


Cost per completed verification How much each completed verification costs


Verification and fraud cost per successfully onboarded customer How much verification and fraud controls cost for each successfully onboarded customer


Fraud alert precision What proportion of investigated fraud alerts is confirmed as fraudulent


Review these metrics monthly and calculate ROI quarterly.


Use the same definitions and measurement windows across reporting periods. Compare fraud losses against transaction volume or value rather than looking at total losses alone.


A business processing twice as many transactions may experience higher total fraud losses even when its fraud loss rate improves.


Similarly, a higher fraud detection rate is only meaningful when the business has reliable data on confirmed fraud, including incidents discovered after the original transaction or verification decision.


These distinctions help finance understand whether the stack is improving fraud prevention, reducing customer friction, or simply processing more activity.


### 5. Avoid These Common ROI Calculation Mistakes


A strong ROI calculation depends on what you count and how you attribute the results.


**Counting only software fees**


Platform charges are not the entire cost. Include the technical, operational, and administrative resources required to run the stack.


**Treating every blocked transaction as prevented fraud**


A blocked event is not automatically fraudulent. Use confirmed fraud outcomes and credible estimates of losses avoided. Otherwise, the reported benefits will be inflated.


**Ignoring false positives**


Incorrectly blocking legitimate customers creates additional review expenses, onboarding abandonment, and lost business. These costs should be reflected in the calculation without duplicating benefits already counted through improved onboarding.


**Using revenue instead of contribution margin**


Additional customer revenue is not a pure financial benefit. Account for the cost of serving those customers before adding their value to ROI.


**Treating productivity improvements as cash savings**


Hours recovered through automation are valuable, but they do not automatically reduce expenditure. Report direct savings and recovered staff capacity separately.


**Counting the same benefit twice**


If an avoided fraud-loss estimate already includes investigation expenses, do not count those same expenses again under operational savings.


**Crediting the technology for every improvement**


Fraud rates and onboarding performance also change because of customer behaviour, transaction volumes, product changes and market conditions. Compare similar periods, account for material differences, and document the assumptions behind your estimates.


A credible ROI report separates observed results from estimated benefits and makes it easy to trace each figure back to its source.

### 7. Build an ROI Report Your Finance Team Can Use


You don't need a complicated financial model to begin measuring ROI. You need consistent data, clear assumptions and a method that accounts for both the cost of fraud prevention and the value it delivers.


Start with a defined reporting period. Calculate the full cost of your identity verification and fraud prevention stack, then measure avoided fraud losses, additional customer contribution and operational efficiencies.


Separate direct financial returns from recovered staff capacity, and document how each benefit was calculated.


The result is more useful than a dashboard showing how many verifications were completed or transactions flagged. It shows whether the investment is reducing losses, improving operations and supporting business growth.

##


### Frequently Asked Questions


-


#### **How do you calculate the ROI of identity verification and fraud prevention?**


Add the financial value of fraud losses avoided, operational savings, additional customer contribution and measurable compliance efficiencies. Subtract the total investment cost, divide by that cost and multiply by 100 to get the ROI percentage. Report productivity benefits separately from direct financial returns.


-


#### **How do you calculate fraud losses avoided?**


Compare your current fraud loss rate against a historical baseline using comparable transaction volumes or values. Adjust for significant business changes and allow for delayed fraud reports before finalising the estimate.


-


#### **What is a good ROI for fraud prevention?**


A positive financial ROI means the measured financial benefits exceed the investment costs. The appropriate target depends on transaction volumes, fraud exposure, operating expenses and the business's risk tolerance. Fraud controls may also be necessary for regulatory or risk-management reasons even when their directly measurable ROI is limited.


-


#### **Should false positives be included in fraud prevention ROI?**


Yes. False positives create additional review costs and can lead to lost customers. Include measurable operational expenses and lost contribution margin resulting from incorrect fraud decisions, without double-counting improvements already included elsewhere.


-


#### **Can identity verification improve customer onboarding ROI?**


Yes. Faster and more effective verification workflows can improve onboarding completion and reduce manual processing costs. Measure the additional customers who become active and calculate their contribution margin to determine the financial benefit.
